references.text: The fat is described as 'food, a fire offering to the Lord', the same expression used in verse 16
The priest burns the fat on the altar as a pleasing aroma to the Lord, the same ritual action
All fat belongs to the Lord and is forbidden to eat, confirming the principle that all fat is the Lord's
The burnt offering is described as a pleasing aroma, a fire offering to the Lord
Noah's sacrifice rose up as a pleasing aroma to the Lord, the first use of the expression 'reiach nichoach'
The fat shall be burned as a fire offering for a pleasing aroma to the Lord
The priest shall sprinkle the blood and burn the fat for a pleasing aroma to the Lord
Paul uses the imagery of a pleasing aroma when he describes Christ's sacrifice for us
It clarifies that the burning of the fat as a 'pleasing aroma' is the very mechanism that enables forgiveness in the sin offering.
Extends the principle of the fat as the Lord's property from the peace offering to also apply to the guilt offering.
Confirms that the rule regarding treating the fat as in the peace offering is a universal norm for all types of offerings requiring atonement.
Partially contrasts (only fat versus the whole animal) to emphasize that 'pleasing aroma' is the common goal for different forms of sacrifice.
Extends the concept of 'pleasing aroma' from animal sacrifices to plant-based gifts, demonstrating universal liturgical unity.
Demonstrates that the requirement for a 'pleasing aroma' applies regardless of the value of the offering or the type of animal.
Adds the dimension of ritual purity (washing) as necessary to achieve the 'pleasing aroma'.
Compares the 'memorial portion' of flour with the 'fat' from animals to show that both represent God's share and create a pleasing aroma.
